extracted.intended_audience: British public and international abolitionist supporters; general readers interested in slavery and anti-slavery advocacy
extracted.subtask_description: Transcripts/excerpts of Frederick Douglass’s mid-19th-century speeches and letters describing the character and cruelties of American slavery and proposing strategies for exposing and abolishing it. Includes appeals to British audiences, moral and legal evidence, and calls for social action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of American slavery
rubrics_metrics.description: “Slavery in the United States is the granting of that power by which one man exercises and enforces a right of property in the body and soul of another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a precise, uncompromising definition emphasizing that the slave is treated as property (marketable commodity), deprived of education, marriage rights, conscience, intellect and affections; contrast with national claims of liberty, Christianity, and justice to reveal hypocrisy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal testimony and lived experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground exposés in first-hand experience and bodily evidence (e.g., marks of the lash, personal history of enslavement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present autobiographical details and bodily evidence to authenticate claims and move audiences emotionally and morally; Douglass repeatedly frames his authority as one who has ‘twenty-one years of my life...spent in slavery’ and bears ‘marks of the lash.’ This serves to rebut denials and to make the abuses tangible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid description of physical cruelties and instruments of torture
rubrics_metrics.description: Catalog and describe the physical punishments and torture devices used (whippings, chains, gag, thumb-screw, cat-o’-nine-tails, blood-hound, branding, fetters, dungeon, starvation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use graphic, specific examples to make the brutality undeniable; cite common practices and give concrete scenes (auctions, brandings, whippings) as persuasive evidence. Reference contemporary accounts (e.g., Dickens) or a ‘testimony of a thousand witnesses’ to corroborate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary proof via slave-state laws and official sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and cite the laws of slaveholding states and legal digests to prove slavery’s sanctioned cruelties and inequalities (e.g., statutes prescribing lashes, branding, execution for colored persons for many offenses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the slaveholders’ own legal codes (Brevard’s Digest; Haywood’s Manual; Virginia Revised Code; Prince’s Digest; Missouri Laws; Mississippi Revised Code) as authoritative evidence; prefer quoting statutes to strengthen claims and preempt objections that abuses are exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose slavery publicly to international audiences to create pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Take the abuses of slavery ‘abroad’—to Britain and other nations—to leverage foreign moral pressure on American slaveholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that publicity and condemnation in Britain (press, pulpit, public meetings) will reverberate back to America and shame or influence slaveholders; emphasize transit/communication improvements (steam) that amplify impact. “Exposing slavery, and it dies” is presented as a central tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to Christian morality and condemn pro‑slave religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish true Christianity (mercy, justice, love to God and man) from the slaveholding, ‘woman-whipping, mind-darkening’ religion that sanctifies slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target ministers and churches that defend slavery, showing how they ‘torture the hallowed pages’ to support the institution. Frame abolition as consistent with genuine Christian doctrine and depict slaveholding religion as its perversion—use this moral contrast to mobilize religious audiences against slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilize press, pulpit, and civil society to foster public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Enlist newspapers, ministers, public meetings, pamphlets, and petitions to create and sustain anti-slavery sentiment and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize events (public breakfasts, ministerial meetings), distribute pamphlets widely (“the pamphlet be bought by tens of thousands”), encourage clergy and press to speak and record denunciations, and foster petitions and organized pressure on American institutions. Emphasize collective, sustained publicity rather than isolated denunciations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevate and improve the condition of free colored people as a means to emancipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Work to promote the moral, social, religious, and intellectual elevation of free colored people in the North as part of the larger strategy to free slaves in the South.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use publishing, education, social organization, personal example, and political participation (voice, pen, vote) to strengthen free blacks’ position and demonstrate progress is possible—this improvement is presented as instrumental to emancipation efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use shocking individual narratives to illustrate systemic cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate singular, tragic stories (e.g., auction of husband and wife, woman leaping from a bridge rather than be recaptured) to exemplify the systemic inhumanity of slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select emblematic, emotionally powerful cases that crystallize the system’s brutality and unjust laws. These narratives function both as moral evidence and as tools for eliciting sympathy and indignation among listeners/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse compromise with individuals or institutions aligned with slaveholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a non-compromising stance toward men and religious figures connected with slaveholders, even at the cost of being maligned or accused of undermining religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to face accusations (infidelity, injuring religion); prioritize the moral obligation to the enslaved (‘the prayers, and tears, and entreaties of three millions of kneeling bondsmen’) over personal popularity or accommodation with pro‑slavery sympathizers.
